steps.title: Collect: crawl the kommun websites
steps.what: A crawler visits the website of each of Sweden's 290 kommuner, one request per second, and keeps the pages about planning and building plus the PDFs they link to (plans, permit guidance, fees...). Limits per kommun: 1,000 pages, 3,000 PDFs, 40 MB per PDF, 15,000 requests.
steps.measure: Coverage: for a sample of kommuner we fetch the list of plans in force that the kommun publishes and count how many of those plans have their PDFs in our corpus. It shows what the crawl misses, which no other test can see.

sections.title: Why listed plan PDFs are missing
sections.text: Read from each kommun's crawl record. The crawler now handles the first two causes (it goes one link deeper from a plan page and takes every on-topic PDF of a plan page, whatever its name): a re-crawl and rebuild bring these PDFs in. Kommuner that publish their plans only in a map need another source (their map service or Lantmäteriet's digital plans), or a browser agent that goes through their map once and lists the plans for the crawler.

steps.title: Filter: remove the PDFs that are not about building
steps.what: A kommun website also links documents unrelated to building: HR policies, school menus, alcohol licences, meeting minutes on other topics. Each PDF is judged in up to three stages: keyword rules on its title and file name, a small classifier trained on those rules, and for every proposed removal a second opinion from an LLM (MiMo Flash, about $0.0001 per PDF). Some were read by hand. No PDF is removed on a rule or the classifier alone: losing a useful document is worse than keeping noise.
steps.measure: Removed PDFs drawn at random and read by hand: how many were useful after all.

steps.title: Read: extract the text, OCR the scans
steps.what: Web pages and PDFs with a text layer are read directly. Scanned PDFs, mostly old plans from the 1950s to the 1990s, are images: they need OCR (optical character recognition) before their text can be searched. The OCR also records where each word sits on the page, so that a property number can be found on a scanned plan map.
steps.measure: OCR engines compared on plan pages: crops of real old scans typed out by hand, and recent plans rendered as images and degraded like a scan (their text layer is the answer key). Score = share of the words read exactly; property numbers like 3:204 are counted apart, they identify a plot.

sections.title: Which OCR engine
sections.text: PP-OCRv6 medium reads 87 % of the words of real scanned plan maps (EasyOCR 69 %) and 8 of 13 property numbers (EasyOCR none: it reads the colon of 3:204 as a dot). It runs free on the laptop's GPU, 5 to 35 s per plan map in the full run. Small text under 12 pixels (zone codes such as e1, b1) stays hard for every engine. Columns: share of the words read exactly, except property numbers.

steps.title: Index: cut into passages, make them searchable
steps.what: Each document is cut into passages of about 1,500 characters (a law: one section per passage), with a header naming the kommun and the document. Each passage gets a vector, a numeric fingerprint of its meaning, so that a question finds passages by meaning; a keyword index finds exact words. Passages repeated across the corpus (standard plan wording) are kept once.
steps.measure: Automatic checks after every rebuild: garbled text, missing law chapters, documents filed under the wrong kommun, passages without a vector, a search store behind the corpus.

sections.title: Why so many documents
sections.text: Plans dominate: a detaljplan is published as a plan map, a description and, for recent plans, consultation reports and studies (noise, traffic, soil...), and many kommun sites also have a web page per plan. Web pages are short (permit guidance, sewage, shore protection); PDFs carry most of the text. Scanned PDFs count as documents but have no passages until the OCR.

steps.title: Plan registry: one record per detaljplan, with its rules
steps.what: Groups the documents of each detaljplan into one plan (name, number, status, documents) and extracts the coded rules printed on the plan (for example e1 = largest building area, h1 = highest building height), so the agent can answer what a plan allows on a plot.
steps.measure: Counts only for now: plans found, plans with their rules extracted. Rules printed only as a map (which zone carries which code) are read by the agent with the image tools.

steps.title: Search: the agent's tools on the corpus
steps.what: The agent answers by exploring the corpus with tools: search by meaning, grep for exact words, read a document, open a law section, list a kommun's documents or plans (each tool in the table below). Their speed sets most of the waiting time outside the model.
steps.measure: Every tool call stored from past benchmark runs is replayed on the current corpus: a call must not fail on something the corpus has, and its time is measured. Times: median (typical call) and 95th percentile (the slow ones).

sections.title: Search quality (retrieval evaluation)
sections.summary: recall@5 88 % on the national corpus, 94 % on the 2026-10-22 one
sections.text: 45 questions written for real use cases (4 kommuner), each labelled with the passages that answer it: recall@5 = share of the expected passages in the first 5 results. The national corpus has three times more passages for these kommuner: no expected passage is missing, but some fall to ranks 7-12 behind other documents of the same kommun (the statutes are unchanged). hybrid-sv-stem is the agent's search.
